title: Two Apple moves behind iOS: Windows iPods and Moore's-law market segmentation
summary: Dalton Caldwell argues two underappreciated Apple tactics built its mobile dominance. Windows-compatible iPods co-opted the Windows userbase and made desktop OS irrelevant, and selling older iPhone models cheaply segmented the market off a single product line, which large rivals struggle to copy because of corporate inertia.

principles.text: Co-opt a rival's installed base by making your product work in their ecosystem, even when it feels off-brand.
principles.quote: By casually co-opting the Windows userbase, Apple made **Windows desktop marketshare irrelevant in the mobile-centric world that would soon come into being.**

principles.text: A first product purchase can be a wedge: the iPod was many people's first Apple device and paved the way for later product lines.
principles.quote: But Windows-compatible iPods paved the way for the iPhone. For iOS. For the iPad.

principles.text: Segment the market off one product line by letting older models become the cheaper tier, instead of building separate products.
principles.quote: Apple is doing market segmentation off of a single product line!

principles.text: One team focused on one great product lets Moore's law turn today's flagship into tomorrow's entry-level device, with no retooling.
principles.quote: They put all of their energy into building the single greatest product they can. Without expending any effort, they simply let Moore’s law transform today’s great product into tomorrow’s entry-level device.

principles.text: Price is a powerful lever: a product nobody could sell at list price flew off shelves at $99.
principles.quote: Lo and behold, the product that they couldn’t sell to save their lives **flew off the shelves** at the $99 price point.

principles.text: Large incumbents often can't copy strategies like this because of corporate inertia: org charts, fiefdoms and existing revenue lines resist consolidation.
principles.quote: However, if I had to take a single guess, I would guess _corporate inertia_.
